generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, the point of this is personal. When a task or an essay feels beyond you, a fixed mindset reads it as a limit, while a growth mindset reads it as something effort and better strategies can improve. Self-efficacy, your belief that you can succeed at a task, shapes whether you take a hard piece of work on or avoid it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students each get a disappointing mark on their first essay.

{{learner-a}} reads the grade and reaches the obvious conclusion: I am not cut out for this subject. The low mark feels like a verdict on fixed ability, so {{learner-a}} quietly avoids the next hard task and stops asking for help, in case it confirms the worst. This is a fixed mindset, and the low self-efficacy that comes with it.

{{learner-b}} is just as disappointed, but reads the mark differently: this attempt did not work, so what can I change? {{learner-b}} studies the feedback, asks the tutor what a stronger essay would do, and treats the next task as a chance to improve. The belief that effort will pay off, rather than being wasted, is self-efficacy at work. This is a growth mindset.

Both students met a setback. Only {{learner-b}} read it as information to act on rather than a limit to accept.
generatedProse.summary: A growth mindset treats ability as something you can build with effort, strategies and feedback, where a fixed mindset treats it as set. Self-efficacy, the belief that you can succeed at a task, is its close partner and shapes whether you take a challenge on. You can now tell the two mindsets apart and identify a growth-mindset response to a setback. The next lesson turns to what drives your effort: your motivation.

check.body: In the worked example, what did {{learner-b}}'s reaction to the low mark show about self-efficacy?

items.text: {{learner-b}} believed effort would pay off, so acted on the feedback to improve.
{{learner-b}} was sure the subject was simply too hard for them.
{{learner-b}} decided the mark proved a lack of ability.
{{learner-b}} avoided the next task in case it went badly.

feedback.correct: That's right. Believing effort would pay off, and acting on it, is self-efficacy.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Self-efficacy is the belief that you can succeed with effort. Which option shows that?
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} showed self-efficacy by trusting that effort would pay off and acting on the feedback. The other options show low self-efficacy.
